facts.text: Star Mark Damon not only played twin brothers Franz and Karl Schiller, he also co-wrote the script as 'Alan M. Harris' — his real birth name was Alan Harris.
Joe D'Amato, the future Emanuelle director, is billed as cinematographer under the English alias 'Michael Holloway'. His real name was Aristide Massaccesi.
Producer Franco Gaudenzi said this was Mark Damon's own project: 'a script he had, it was his creature.' Damon planned to sell it to an American distributor.
The score is by Vasili Kojucharov. Kim Newman, reviewing the film in 2020, called it a 'euro-lounge score.'
Only Luigi Batzella got the director credit, but producer Franco Gaudenzi said Joe D'Amato (later of Emanuelle fame) also directed, reshooting some scenes.
Kim Newman's review says the plot borrows from Hammer's Scars of Dracula, the Countess Dracula and Karnstein films, and even the American Count Yorga vampire movies.
Mark Damon was so impressed by Joe D'Amato that he recommended him to Roger Corman for the American production The Arena (1974).
TV Guide's review called it 'ineptly made, fairly gory, and with lots of nudity' — most of it from Rosalba Neri (credited as Sara Bay) — and said Countess Bathory's real story is more interesting.
Rosalba Neri said of director Luigi Batzella: 'It was like there were two of them, going different directions... A bit schizophrenic, indeed.'
Moria's Richard Scheib places the film in the 'Continental Gothic' cycle that grew out of Hammer, Roger Corman's Poe films and Mario Bava's Black Sunday. He gave it two stars.
Shooting began July 31, 1972 at Castello Piccolomini in Balsorano, Italy — a castle that also appeared in Lady Frankenstein, Bloody Pit of Horror and Crypt of the Vampire.
Moria notes that star Mark Damon wrote the English script as 'Alan M. Harris' — the only time he used that name — with producer Ralph Zucker adapting the dialogue.
Italian censors gave it an under-18 rating and demanded cuts: a shortened first love scene and no scenes where 'the man kisses the lower part of the woman's body.'
Reviewer Dave Sindelar says the film mashes up the Nibelungen legend, Dracula, Countess Bathory and Edgar Allan Poe, plus abstract footage that seems to echo 2001: A Space Odyssey.
The 1974 French release, titled Les vierges de la pleine lune, restored the footage Italian censors had cut from the lesbian scene between Rosalba Neri and Esmeralda Barros.
In the US the film was handled by Dimension Pictures in theaters, and later on home video by Wizard Video and VCI. In Italy it opened through the distributor Regionale.
The Italian title, Il plenilunio delle vergini, means 'Full Moon of the Virgins.' The English title sells it as a Devil-worship film, riding the early-70s occult craze.
The film got the Elvira's Movie Macabre treatment: Shout! Factory released it in 2006 in that line, but with the nudity removed. Code Red's 2021 Blu-ray restored it from the US version.
Moria's Richard Scheib noted the amusing touch that the amulet is tied to Pazuzu, an obscure Mesopotamian demon popularised by The Exorcist (1973).
DVD Talk's Ian Jane called it 'enjoyable enough' and said of star Rosalba Neri's Countess: 'She is the show,' with director Luigi Batzella wisely capitalizing on her screen presence.
The film grossed 117,115,000 lire in Italy. Its theatrical premiere was April 10, 1973 at the Politeama in Torre Annunziata.
DVD Talk says the film was made 'fast and cheap' to cash in on Italy's gothic horror craze of the early 1970s.
Film historian Gary A. Smith, in Vampire Films of the 1970s, called it 'a throwback to gothic horror' that seems influenced by Hammer's Twins of Evil (1971).
The film has also circulated under the titles Full Moon of the Virgins and, in French, Les Vierges Maudites de Dracula ('Dracula's Cursed Virgins').
Rosalba Neri is credited as 'Sara Bay.' She also played the title role in Lady Frankenstein (1971), another gothic horror shot at the same castle.
Luigi Batzella's director credit varies by print: 'Paul Solvay' in English credits, with the Italian script credited to Walter Bigari and Paolo Solvay, both names tied to Batzella.
Mark Damon starred in Roger Corman's House of Usher (1960), winning a Golden Globe for New Star of the Year, then moved to Italy for spaghetti westerns.
Mark Damon later became a major producer: The Lost Boys, Short Circuit, 9½ Weeks and Das Boot all came from his companies. Star Damon is also cousin to composer Danny Elfman.
The Italian script was reportedly adapted from 'The Brides of Countess Dracula' by Ian Danby and Ralph Zucker; the film credits director 'Paul Solvay' for Luigi Batzella.
An early draft script opened with a prologue not in the film: the Countess summons evil while nude women are tied to a column and have their throats slashed.
Director Luigi Batzella also made Nude for Satan (1974) and the Nazisploitation film SS Hell Camp (1977), working under many pseudonyms.
Sergio Pislar is credited as Karl, but Mark Damon played both twins; Pislar reportedly doubled in two-shots, with split-screen covering other shared scenes.
Xiro Papas, who plays the vampire monster, also played the monster in the Italian cult film Frankenstein '80 (1972).
Film appears in Piecing Together Lady Frankenstein (2018), a documentary about Rosalba Neri's Lady Frankenstein.
